q: How does the spine move in yoga?
What are the six movements of the spine?
What is axial extension in yoga?
How do I protect my spine during yoga?
What are the different regions of the spine?
What is the sacroiliac joint and how does yoga affect it?
How do I find a neutral spine in yoga poses?
a: The spine has six primary movements utilized in yoga: forward bending (flexion), backward bending (extension), side bending (lateral flexion to the left and right), and twisting (rotation to the left and right). The spinal column is divided into five regions: cervical (7 vertebrae in the neck), thoracic (12 vertebrae with rib attachments), lumbar (5 weight-bearing vertebrae in the lower back), sacrum (5 fused vertebrae connecting to the pelvis), and coccyx (4 fused vertebrae at the tailbone). Axial extension—lengthening the spine by creating space between the vertebrae—is a foundational principle in yoga that decompresses the discs and protects the spine during movement. A neutral spine maintains the natural curves of the spine without excessive flattening or arching, and is the safest position for most weight-bearing poses. The sacroiliac (SI) joint connects the sacrum to the ilium bones of the pelvis; SI joint instability or inflammation requires avoiding asymmetrical standing poses and deep twists until the joint stabilizes.

q: What is the anatomy of the hip joint in yoga?
What are the six movements of the hip?
How do I open my hips safely in yoga?
What is hip impingement (FAI) and how does yoga help?
How does yoga affect psoas muscle?
What yoga poses stretch the piriformis?
What is hip instability in yoga?
a: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint where the femoral head articulates with the acetabulum of the pelvis, allowing six movements essential in yoga: flexion (forward fold, knee to chest), extension (backbend, standing leg back), abduction (leg out to side, standing wide-legged), adduction (leg across midline, eagle pose), internal rotation (leg turns inward, warrior II front leg), and external rotation (leg turns outward, pigeon pose). Hip impingement (femoroacetabular impingement or FAI) involves bone spurs on the femoral head or acetabulum that catch during deep flexion or rotation—practicing with external rotation before deep flexion and avoiding forced range of motion can help manage symptoms. The psoas major muscle runs from the lumbar spine to the femur, functioning as both a hip flexor and a spinal stabilizer; tight psoas is linked to lower back pain and can be released through gentle lunges and supine knee-to-chest poses. Piriformis syndrome, where the piriformis muscle compresses the sciatic nerve, responds well to supine figure-four stretches and gentle pigeon pose modifications.

q: What is the anatomy of the shoulder joint in yoga?
What is scapulohumeral rhythm?
How do I protect my shoulders in yoga?
What is shoulder impingement in yoga?
What is the rotator cuff and how does yoga strengthen it?
What is scapular winging?
How do I stabilize my shoulders in weight-bearing poses?
a: The shoulder (glenohumeral) joint is a highly mobile ball-and-socket joint where the humeral head articulates with the shallow glenoid fossa of the scapula, prioritizing mobility over stability. Scapulohumeral rhythm describes the coordinated movement between the glenohumeral joint and the scapula during arm elevation—for every two degrees of arm raising, approximately one degree comes from scapular upward rotation. The rotator cuff consists of four muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) that stabilize the humeral head within the glenoid; yoga poses like downward dog, plank, and forearm balance strengthen these muscles when practiced with proper alignment—engaging the serratus anterior to keep the shoulder blades spread and stable. Shoulder impingement occurs when the rotator cuff tendons or bursa are pinched between the humeral head and the acromion, often aggravated by repetitively lowering in chaturanga without proper scapular stability (scapular winging or lack of serratus engagement). Key alignment cues include externally rotating the upper arms in weight-bearing poses, drawing the shoulder blades down the back, and never letting the shoulders collapse toward the ears.

q: What is the anatomy of the knee in yoga?
How do I protect my knees in yoga poses?
What is the Q angle and how does it affect yoga?
What is patellofemoral pain syndrome in yoga?
How does yoga affect the meniscus?
What is genu valgum and genu varum?
What yoga poses are safe for knee injuries?
a: The knee is primarily a hinge joint (flexion and extension) between the femur and tibia, with the patella (kneecap) gliding in the patellofemoral groove during movement. In yoga, knee alignment is critical because the joint relies on surrounding muscles (quadriceps, hamstrings, gastrocnemius) and ligaments (ACL, PCL, MCL, LCL) for stability rather than bony structure. The Q angle is the angle between the quadriceps tendon and patellar tendon—individuals with a larger Q angle (more common in women) may be more prone to patellar tracking issues and should engage the vastus medialis oblique (inner quad) to stabilize the kneecap. Genu valgum (knock knees) and genu varum (bow legs) affect how weight distributes through the knee joint; in both cases, tracking the knee over the second and third toes in bent-leg poses (warrior I and II, lunges) is essential to prevent medial or lateral stress. To protect knees in yoga, avoid hyperextending standing legs, engage the quadriceps actively in straight-leg poses, never force the foot to the opposite thigh in lotus (use half-lotus or a simple cross-legged position instead), and use blankets under the knees in kneeling poses.

q: What are the bandhas in yoga?
What is Mula Bandha (root lock)?
What is Uddiyana Bandha (abdominal lock)?
What is Jalandhara Bandha (chin lock)?
How do bandhas support core stability?
What is Maha Bandha?
How do the bandhas affect energy in yoga practice?
a: Bandhas are energetic locks or seals in yoga that direct the flow of prana (life force energy) and provide structural stability to the body. Mula Bandha (root lock) involves engaging the perineum and pelvic floor muscles, drawing them upward—it stabilizes the pelvis, supports the spine from below, and is often maintained throughout asana practice. Uddiyana Bandha (abdominal lift) is performed after a full exhalation by drawing the navel back toward the spine and lifting the abdominal organs upward under the rib cage—it massages the internal organs, strengthens the transverse abdominis, and supports the lower back. Jalandhara Bandha (chin lock) is performed by lowering the chin toward the chest while lifting the sternum—it regulates blood flow to the heart and brain and is primarily used during pranayama practice. Maha Bandha (great lock) combines all three bandhas simultaneously, creating a full-body energetic seal that contains and channels prana. Together, the bandhas build intra-abdominal pressure, protect the spine in challenging poses, lighten the body for inversions and arm balances, and deepen meditative focus.
